html:
Holstein was a duchy in the far north of Germany, between the Elbe and the Eider rivers, with Kiel as its main town. It was the northernmost land of the Holy Roman Empire, yet for centuries its duke was the king of Denmark.

That double position is the whole story of Holstein. Its neighbour Schleswig was a Danish fief, while Holstein was German; the two duchies were bound together by old promises. After 1815 Holstein belonged to the German Confederation while still ruled from Copenhagen.

In the 1800s Danish and German nationalists both claimed the duchies. Denmark tried to tie Schleswig more closely to the kingdom, and in 1864 Prussia and Austria went to war against it in the Second Schleswig War. Denmark lost both duchies. Bismarck then used a quarrel over their rule to start the Austro-Prussian War of 1866, after which Prussia annexed Holstein. The Kiel Canal later cut across it.
